key.title: Acquiring Confidence Before an Audience
key.main_idea: Fear of speaking in public is overcome by speaking, not by reading about it. Face audiences often, fill your mind with your subject instead of yourself, prepare well, and expect to succeed.

key_lessons.text: You learn to speak by speaking. Frequent practice in front of people is the cure for fear.
key_lessons.source_snippet: You must learn to speak by speaking.

key_lessons.text: Even great speakers felt stage-fright; it is not a sign that you are unfit to speak.
key_lessons.source_snippet: Daniel Webster failed in his first appearance and had to take his seat without finishing his speech because he was nervous.

key_lessons.text: Get absorbed in your subject. When your mind is full of your message, there is no room left for fear.
key_lessons.source_snippet: fill your mind with your speech-material and, like the infilling water in the glass, it will drive out your unsubstantial fears

key_lessons.text: Have something worth saying and prepare it, including your first few sentences.
key_lessons.source_snippet: Have the first few sentences worked out completely

key_lessons.text: After preparing, expect success. Your audience usually wants you to do well.
key_lessons.source_snippet: a hundred chances to one they want you to succeed

key.takeaway: Prepare well, think about your message instead of yourself, and then speak as often as you can. Confidence grows from practice, not from waiting to feel ready.

quick_check.question: What is the authors' main cure for fear of speaking?
options: Speak before audiences as often as you can
Read many books about public speaking first
Avoid speaking until the fear goes away
quick_check.simpler_explanation: Like learning to swim, you only lose the fear by getting into the water. Speak in front of people again and again, and the fear gets smaller.

reflection_questions: When did fear stop you from speaking up, at work, in a meeting or with family?
What subject do you care about so much that you forget yourself when you talk about it?
What is one small chance this week to speak in front of others?

examples.text: The authors compare it to horses near a railway: the ones that see trains every day keep grazing, while a horse that rarely sees one panics.

examples.text: One way to get air out of a glass is to pour in water: fill your mind with your subject and the fear is pushed out.

examples.text: A new team leader who volunteers to give the two-minute update at every weekly meeting will be far calmer by the third month.

complete.title: Acquiring Confidence Before an Audience
complete.main_idea: Fear of speaking in public is overcome by speaking, not by reading about it. Face audiences often, fill your mind with your subject instead of yourself, prepare well, and expect to succeed.

sections.heading: Face the audience often
sections.explanation: Students keep asking how to overcome fear before an audience. The answer is "horse-sense": a horse gets used to trains by seeing them often, and a speaker gets used to audiences by facing them often. Reading about it is not enough; you have to plunge in.

examples.source_snippet: some horses feed near the track and never even pause to look up at the thundering cars

examples.text: The "wetless" bathing suit nobody ever learned to swim in.
examples.source_snippet: There are a great many "wetless" bathing suits worn at the seashore, but no one ever learns to swim in them.

sections.heading: Fear is normal, even for great speakers
sections.explanation: Do not be discouraged if you feel stage-fright. Sensitive people feel it more. Famous speakers like Daniel Webster, Gladstone and Beecher all struggled with nerves; Webster even had to sit down without finishing his first speech.

examples.source_snippet: Daniel Webster failed in his first appearance and had to take his seat without finishing his speech because he was nervous.

sections.heading: Be absorbed by your subject
sections.explanation: Concentration means being distracted from less important things. If you care deeply about your subject and fill your mind with it, worries about your clothes or your image are pushed out, the way water pushes air out of a glass. Think of yourself as a messenger with a message, not as an exhibit.

examples.text: If a theatre caught fire, you would shout directions without any self-consciousness, because the message matters more than you.
examples.source_snippet: If the theater caught fire you could rush to the stage and shout directions to the audience without any self-consciousness

sections.heading: Have something to say
sections.explanation: Many speakers walk up with an empty mind, and it fills with worries like "How does my hair look?" Prepare: know your subject better than your listeners, know roughly how you will say it, and have your first few sentences worked out completely.

sections.heading: Expect success and take charge
sections.explanation: After preparing, expect to succeed. Believing you will fail almost guarantees it, as when Washington Irving told a friend, "I told you I would fail, and I did." Pause, look at your audience, and remember they want you to succeed.

examples.text: Irving at the dinner for Dickens.
examples.source_snippet: There, I told you I would fail, and I did.

sections.heading: Final hints
sections.explanation: Do not rush to begin, and do not apologise. Take a deep breath, relax, and start in a quiet, conversational tone, as if speaking to one large friend. Like a cold plunge, it is much easier once you are in.
